What terminal apply states mean, which ones have a way back, and how to recover
when a schema change fails. Written for operators and for agents driving
SchemaBot through the CLI, API, or PR comments.

## Foundations

SchemaBot is declarative: you describe the schema you *want* in SQL files, and
SchemaBot works out how to get your database there. Three concepts carry this
document:

- **Plan** — the diff between your desired schema and the live database,
  computed as an ordered list of DDL statements. A plan says "here is the work
  needed to converge." Planning is read-only; nothing changes until an apply.
- **Apply** — one execution of a plan. Each apply gets its own identifier and
  is tracked as a record in SchemaBot's own bookkeeping database (separate from
  the database being changed). That record moves through states — from
  `pending` through `running` to a final verdict — and it is what you see in
  CLI status output and PR comments.
- **Driver** — the component inside SchemaBot that claims an apply and drives it
  to a final state, reporting progress along the way. If a driver crashes, a
  peer picks the apply up and continues; the apply record is the durable truth,
  not any single process.

```
 schema files (desired)      live database (actual)
          \                       /
           \                     /
            v                   v
          plan  =  the DDL needed to converge
            |
            |   operator confirms
            v
          apply = one tracked execution of that plan
            |
            |   driven by a driver, progress recorded
            v
        a final verdict: completed, failed, cancelled,
                         reverted, or stopped
```

### The record tree

Every schema change becomes one record tree: **Plan → Apply → Operation →
Task**. An apply bundles one or more DDL statements — everything the PR changes
for that database ships together. It expands into **operations** (one per
deployment — the unit a driver claims) and each operation into **tasks** (one
per statement).

```
 plan                        the diff — DDL + original schema (for rollback)
   └─ apply                  "apply plan-123 to staging" — state derived below
        ├─ operation         one per deployment/target — lease, resume state
        │    ├─ task         ALTER TABLE users ... (rows copied, %, ETA)
        │    └─ task         one per DDL statement (per shard on sharded Vitess)
        ├─ control requests  durable operator commands — stop/start/cancel,
        │                    cutover, release, revert/skip-revert
        ├─ apply logs        audit trail — powers `schemabot logs`
        └─ comments          tracked PR comments — progress + summary recovery

 checks   per-database rows -> one aggregate GitHub Check Run
```

Three properties of the tree matter for everything below:

- **State flows upward.** A driver writes only its own operation; the parent
  apply's state is *derived* from all of its operations, never written
  directly. Sibling operations — other deployments, other shards — are each
  claimed by whichever driver gets there first (on the same pod or different
  ones) and run in parallel without clobbering each other.
- **The tree is the recovery record.** Engine resume state lives on the
  operation, control requests and logs live beside it, and the PR-comment
  observer is rebuilt from the apply's GitHub context. A fresh pod can pick up
  the whole picture from storage.
- **One active apply per target.** Enforced in the storage write path per
  (database, type, environment) — you cannot start a second apply against a
  target that already has one in flight.

### Active vs terminal

An apply's states split into two families:

- **Active** — work is in flight or eligible to be picked up (`pending`,
  `running`, `waiting_for_cutover`, `failed_retryable`, ...).
- **Terminal** — the apply has its verdict (`completed`, `failed`,
  `cancelled`, `reverted`, `stopped`).

## The one rule

**A finished apply stays finished.** Once an apply reaches a terminal state,
that record is history: SchemaBot never turns it back into in-flight work. Not
by retrying it, not through an API call, and not when a crashed driver comes
back and writes stale progress — the bookkeeping database rejects any write
that would flip a terminal apply back to an active state.

To keep going after a failure, you either resume a *stopped* apply through its
dedicated resume command (the one sanctioned way back), or you start over with
a **new plan and a new apply**.

Starting over is not wasteful, because plans are diffs. A fresh plan after a
partial failure compares your desired schema against the database *as it is
now* — including whatever the failed apply already finished — so it contains
only the remaining work. Statements that landed are not re-run. There is
nothing a "retry this exact apply" operation could do that a fresh plan and
apply does not do better.

## State reference

| State | Terminal? | What it means | Way back |
|---|---|---|---|
| `completed` | yes | The schema change landed. | None needed. |
| `failed` | yes | The apply failed permanently (recovery retries exhausted, or the failure is not retryable). | New plan + apply. |
| `cancelled` | yes | An operator cancelled the apply. | New plan + apply. |
| `reverted` | yes | The change was rolled back inside the engine's revert window. | New plan + apply. |
| `stopped` | yes, but resumable | An operator stopped the apply. Engine checkpoints are preserved. | `start` control command — the one guarded transition out of a terminal state. |
| `failed_retryable` | **no** | A transient failure (for example, repeated inability to read progress from the data plane). The apply is paused, still visible, and still blocking. | Automatic: recovery drivers reclaim and retry it, within the retry budget below. |

```
                   +------------------- active ----------------------+
                   |                                                 |
 plan + confirm -->| pending --> running --> ... --> cutting_over    |--> completed
                   |               |  ^                              |--> failed
                   |               v  | automatic                    |--> cancelled
                   |      failed_retryable                           |--> reverted
                   |       (recovery retries;                        |
                   |        exhausted --> failed)                    |--> stopped
                   |                                                 |      |
                   +----------------------^--------------------------+      |
                                          |                                 |
                                          +------- start (resume) ---------+
```

`stopped` is terminal for claiming — no driver picks it up on its own — but it
is the deliberate pause state: resuming through the `start` command re-checks
that no other apply is active on the same target, then hands the work to a
fresh driver, continuing from engine checkpoints rather than starting over.

## The retry budget

Not every failure is final. Some failures are *transient*: the schema change
itself is fine, but something around it hiccupped — a dropped connection to the
data plane, a network blip, an unclean kill mid-drive. Nothing about the work
needs to change; it just needs to be picked up again. Those failures move the
apply to `failed_retryable` instead of `failed`, and recovery is automatic: a
recovery driver reclaims the apply and continues it from where it left off,
using engine checkpoints so completed work is not redone. Failures where
retrying cannot help — the engine rejected a statement, the target refused the
change — skip this state and go straight to permanent `failed`.

A clean shutdown is not one of these failures. A process that stops on purpose
hands its claims back and leaves the apply active, so a peer driver resumes it
without the apply ever passing through `failed_retryable` or spending budget.

Each automatic pickup consumes one **recovery attempt** from a fixed budget —
currently **10 attempts**, on top of the original run. The attempt counter is
visible in the PR progress comment, so you can watch how much budget an apply
has burned.

```
 running --(recoverable failure)--> failed_retryable
    ^                                     |
    |     recovery driver reclaims,       |
    +---- attempt counter +1, resume <----+
          from checkpoints                |
                                          |  budget spent (10 attempts),
                                          |  or the failure is older than
                                          |  the recovery window (1 day)
                                          v
                                   failed  (permanent)
```

Two things end the loop:

- **The budget runs out.** Ten consecutive recoveries that each failed again
  is a strong signal the problem is not transient — retrying an eleventh time
  would just burn resources on the same wall.
- **The recovery window closes.** A `failed_retryable` apply that has been
  sitting for more than a day is no longer picked up automatically, even with
  budget to spare. This prevents a surprise: an old paused failure silently
  springing back to life days later (for example, after a configuration change
  restores connectivity). Old failures deserve a deliberate decision, not an
  automatic redispatch.

Either way, the apply is then terminalized as permanent `failed`, and the
normal recovery path applies: fix the cause, fresh plan, fresh apply. The
budget and window are per-apply — a new apply starts with a full budget.

## Recovering from a failed apply

```
 apply state?
   |
   +-- failed_retryable --> wait; recovery retries it automatically
   |
   +-- stopped ----------> `start` resumes it from checkpoints
   |
   +-- failed / cancelled / reverted
             |
             v
      1. read the failure, fix the cause if there is one
             |
             v
      2. run a fresh plan          (diffs desired schema vs the live
             |                      database; already-landed work is
             v                      not in the diff)
      3. apply the fresh plan      (a NEW apply, new identifier)
```

1. **Confirm the state.** Check the apply's status (CLI status command, or the
   summary comment on the PR). `failed_retryable` needs no action — recovery
   retries it automatically. Only permanent `failed` needs you.
2. **Read the failure.** The apply's own log stream carries the cause, each
   paused attempt with the recovery budget it had left, and the reason recovery
   gave up — read it from the CLI (`schemabot logs <apply>`) or the PR summary
   comment, no infrastructure access required. The server logs, keyed by the
   apply identifier, are there when you need what happened around the apply
   rather than to it. Fix the underlying cause if there is one — an invalid
   statement, a permissions problem, an unreachable target.
3. **Plan again.** Run a fresh plan against the same schema and environment
   (`schemabot plan`, or a new `schemabot plan` PR comment). The plan reflects
   whatever the failed apply already completed: tables that landed are not in
   the diff, and only the remaining work is.
4. **Apply the fresh plan.** This is a new apply with its own identifier and
   its own lifecycle. The failed apply stays in history as the record of what
   happened.

Do not try to edit, re-drive, or re-submit the failed apply itself. There is no
supported operation that reopens it, and API writes that would do so are
refused.

## What cleans up after a failed rollout

A rollout that spans multiple deployments can fail with some per-deployment
operation rows never started. A background reaper settles those rows by
mirroring the parent apply's verdict onto them once the parent has been settled
and quiet for a short quiescence window. Operators do not need to clean these
up by hand; a `pending` operation row under a long-settled parent resolving
itself is normal.

Rows under a `stopped` or `failed_retryable` parent are left alone — they
belong to the resume and recovery paths.

## Guidance for agents

- Treat terminal states as facts, not obstacles. If an apply is `failed`,
  `cancelled`, or `reverted`, the next action is always a fresh plan — never a
  mutation of the existing apply.
- `failed_retryable` means wait. Recovery is automatic; re-planning while it is
  still retrying will be blocked because the apply still counts as active on
  its target.
- Use the apply identifier (the user-facing string, not a numeric row ID) when
  querying status, reading logs, or issuing control commands.
- Control commands (`stop`, `start`, `cancel`, `cutover`, and the rest) are the
  only supported way to influence a live apply. They are recorded durably
  before they are acknowledged, so a command survives pod restarts and lease
  handovers — issue it once and watch the status or PR comment for the effect.
